title: The Khalsa's greeting
hookLine: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh: the Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory

cards: A speaker steps up to the microphone in a gurdwara. Before a single word of the talk, they put their palms together and say: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh.

And the whole congregation says it straight back to them, word for word. Only then does the talk begin. Two friends meet at the door afterward and say the same thing, sometimes shortened to just fateh.
It sounds like a formality. It's actually a small statement about who wins.

teach.b: Take the two halves. Waheguru ji ka Khalsa: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru.

The Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs that Guru Gobind Singh founded at Anandpur on Vaisakhi in 1699, and tradition explains the word khalsa as pure, belonging directly to the sovereign with no middleman.
Then Waheguru ji ki fateh: the victory belongs to Waheguru. Fateh means victory.
Sikh tradition links this greeting to the founding of the Khalsa, and the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, gives it as the greeting Sikhs use with one another. Now, the twist.
A greeting about victory could easily turn into bragging: we win. This one does the opposite.
It hands the victory away the moment it's spoken. Whatever goes well, the exam, the deal, the hard conversation, the battle in older times, the greeting says it isn't the speaker's. It's Waheguru's.
And the people saying it don't belong to themselves either. So two people greeting each other this way remind each other, every time, of two things: you are not your own, and the credit is not yours.
Some Sikhs describe it as freeing instead: if the victory is God's, then so, in a way, is the pressure. A person can work as hard as they're able, then let the outcome rest where it belongs.
And it's said back, word for word. Neither person is above the other in this greeting. Both are equally God's.

how: Sikhs greet one another, and open talks in the gurdwara, with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh; the listener replies with the same words.

o: the name of the Khalsa's founding day
a polite hello with no deeper meaning
victory, which the greeting gives to God

games.q: the Khalsa's greeting — tap the pairs.

s: the greeting claims victory for the Khalsa
it hands the victory to Waheguru: Waheguru ji ki fateh.
the person greeted replies with the same words
neither is above the other; both are God's.
the greeting is often shortened to just fateh
friends at the door sometimes say only that: victory.

games.q: you've just won something big. you greet a friend the way the Khalsa does. whose is the victory?
games.why: Waheguru ji ki fateh: the victory belongs to God, and so do the people who say it.

practice: Think of one thing that went well for you recently, something you might be quietly proud of, and picture it clearly.

Without dismissing your effort, imagine handing the credit forward, to the people who helped, to the chances you were given, and, if you pray, to the One, and notice whether that feels like a loss or a relief.
If you're comfortable, say the greeting once, softly: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh.

wordCard.voice: Fateh. Victory. In the Khalsa's greeting, Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, both the community and the victory belong to God.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: victory; the last word of the Khalsa's greeting.

carryVoice: Your line: the victory is his. Said back, word for word, between equals. Day six hundred thirty-eight.
